title: A Bull Market, Fueled by Pikachu, Charizard and Nostalgia
html:
Scott Pratte turned his boyhood hobby into his livelihood. But he doesn’t usually tell people he’s a Pokémon card collector.

In conversations, he is vague about what he does for a living, saying his business involves collectibles or investments.

“I wouldn’t want to share numbers on the record,” Mr. Pratte, 39, said in an interview, though he noted that the past few years have been “million-dollar years in earnings.”

Pokémon originated as a pair of video games released in Japan for Nintendo’s Game Boy console in 1996. The franchise expanded to include a trading card game, released the same year, which came to the United States in 1999. That’s when Mr. Pratte and others first marveled at the artwork, swapped cards on playgrounds and obsessed over completing sets they shrouded in plastic sleeves in protective binders.

As Pokémon has grown — on its 30th anniversary, the franchise now spans TV shows and films, all manner of merchandise and a stable of more than 1,000 “pocket monsters” — the cards have skyrocketed in value.
summary: On the 30th anniversary of the franchise, Pokémon cards are skyrocketing in value — to the point that collecting them isn’t just big business, it’s a viable livelihood.
